Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn The leaders of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), the National Liberal Party (PNL), the Save Romania Union (USR), and the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR) will meet on August 11 with president Nicuşor Dan to discuss the draft of the Wage Law for the budgetary sector, according to Digi24 . The meeting at Cotroceni Palace, scheduled to take place in the afternoon, will bring together PSD president Sorin Grindeanu, PNL president and interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan, USR president Dominic Fritz, and UDMR president Kelemen Hunor, alongside representatives of the parties involved in the working group preparing the legislation. The four parties previously formed Romania's ruling coalition but have failed to reach an agreement on the wage reform. Trade unions have also refused consultations on the draft and have staged protests against the proposed changes. Interim Minister of Labour Dragoş Pîslaru said on August 10 that this week represents the final opportunity to reach a political agreement that would allow the legislation to be adopted and promulgated before the August 31 deadline under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR). The Wage Law is a PNRR milestone linked to a EUR 771 million grant. Failure to complete the milestone by the set deadline could put the associated European funding at risk. The legislation is intended to establish a new framework for remuneration in Romania's public sector, with the government seeking to link wage developments to fiscal consolidation and the country's commitments under the PNRR. Andrew Tate has been indicted in Romania on new charges involving allegations of having sex with a minor, human trafficking, and money laundering. The 39-year-old influencer was charged alongside his brother, Tristan Tate, as the pair remain in federal detention in Florida. They both face extradition proceedings to the United Kingdom over the alleged crimes, and Tristan has been charged with complicity in connection with the investigation. Tate has also been accused of recruiting a 15-year-old girl and sexually exploiting her in the UK and Romania. Prosecutors allege that he forced the girl to create sexually explicit material, while Tristan Tate allegedly managed the girl’s video chat accounts and monitored her activities. Prosecutors further allege that he “resorted to acts of physical aggression” against the victim. The brothers are accused of making over $1.25 million in their criminal activity. Additionally, Tate is accused of having sex with another 15-year-old girl in Romania in 2020 and 2021. Attorney Eugen Constantin Vidineac has said that the pair “continue to reject the allegations against them.” “Today’s decision by DIICOT does not determine guilt and it should not be presented as though it does. It represents the prosecution’s latest attempt to bring this case before a court following the failure of its previous indictment to proceed to trial,” he said, according to the New York Post . “The history of these proceedings matters. The previous indictment was subjected to judicial scrutiny and the court identified significant irregularities which prevented the case from moving forward to trial." “DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process,” the attorney added. The attorney has also said that the brothers are concerned that their continued incarceration in the US could result in them being found guilty in Romania. Tate expressed concerns that he could face a life sentence in Romania while being detained in the US, and Tristan noted he does not have the ability to prove innocence due to incarceration. “I need to clear my name,” Tristan said. “I need to take part in these proceedings, I can’t do that from the secure housing unit.” Image: Title: Tate Popular View All BREAKING: Trump makes deal with Denmark giving US control over security in Greenland Saudi ARAMCO tells European refiners they won't get any oil in October after pipeline destroyed in Iraqi militant, Houthi attacks LIBBY EMMONS: Backlash to Sydney Sweeney's nude ad shows failure of feminism First female Archbishop of Canterbury forced to revoke 'Interfaith Cooperation' award she gave to terrorist sympathizer KANGMIN LEE to JACK POSOBIEC: It is a 'desecration' of C.S. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz6z.text: Image caption, Hayden Leigh, a forensic science graduate at the University of Staffordshire, has been studying the hair of Boris the bear By Richard Price West Midlands Published 6 September 2026 A student has been using hair from a 120-year-old museum exhibit to help find new ways of solving wildlife crime. The taxidermy bear, known as Boris, is a popular feature at the Museum of Chelmsford and is regarded as its unofficial mascot. Hayden Leigh, a forensic science graduate at the University of Staffordshire, is using samples taken from his hair to help protect modern-day brown bears from illegal poaching. His PhD research involves analysing Boris's fur to compare how its characteristics could improve identification of animal hairs during investigations. Boris arrived at the museum in 1932 amongst a large collection of taxidermy bequeathed by a local game hunter. Leigh said in the wild the animals were mostly found in places like Romania and Bulgaria as well as Russia. He said he had been using a microscope to analyse the cuticles, and different layers of the bear's fur as well as its DNA. Leigh had previously approached about 30 zoos and museums for help with the project before the Museum of Chelmsford said they would lend a hand. "There's been hundreds of studies done on dog hairs and cat hairs and general domestic animals, and I thought, well, let's make a wider impact than on the wider wildlife crime investigations," he said. Image caption, Boris the bear is a popular exhibit at the Museum of Chelmsford in Essex By developing more a cost-effective and reliable alternative to DNA analysis, the aim is to help tackle the illegal poaching and trafficking of wildlife. "Taxidermy samples from museums can play a valuable role in the research of animal hair within a forensic context, Leigh added. "They are often far more accessible than obtaining hair from live animals. "In my project, I examined Boris's hair at a microscopic level, assessing the characteristics of the hairs and investigating whether there was any variation across different areas of the body." Having access to a preserved specimen had also meant an opportunity to examine authentic animal hair in a controlled and ethical way, he said, without needing to disturb a live animal. Councillor Jennie Lardge, cabinet member for culture and leisure at Chelmsford City Council, acknowledged that taxidermy was often considered a controversial part of museum collections, but said it was "wonderful" that Boris' legacy would be to help protect other animals from illegal hunting. "It highlights the scientific value of historic taxidermy collections in museums in 2026, and we are delighted that the Museum of Chelmsford has been able to support this important project," she said. https://www.dw.com/en/as-russia-steps-up.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nv2l Data centers are essential for maintaining online services Image: Serjunco/Westend61/IMAGO Advertisement Hackers and power outages were once the largest threat to Ukraine's data centers. Now, it is the buildings themselves that are in the cross hairs. Since early September, Russia has been targeting these centers, which house the physical infrastructure needed to store digital information, systematically. Digital infrastructure in and around the capital Kyiv was already affected but after the attacks, several television channels and streaming services were temporarily unavailable. Subscribers to several cable networks also reported that they had difficulties connecting. Why is Russia targeting Ukrainian data centers? The servers and computer systems needed to store data and keep online services operating smoothly are a crucial target because if they are damaged, it can have a nationwide effect. All online systems, ranging from news portals, state registries, banking and finance, need functioning data centers to operate smoothly. Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said Russia had targeted major Ukrainian data centers to disrupt the flow of information. "As Russia isn’t achieving its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians." Has Russia changed its approach in its war with Ukraine? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Could Ukraine go offline? Despite widespread damage caused by Russian attacks , experts do not believe the country risks having a complete internet blackout. Telecommunications expert Oleksandr Glushchenko told DW that this was because the entire sector was quite decentralized. "The industry was never regulated in Ukraine, and no multi-million licenses were required,” he explained. "Entering the market was very affordable, which is why thousands of businesses started offering their services." He added that Ukrainians could choose between multiple providers — and in some cases up to 10. This competition, he said, meant that Ukraine had "some of the best internet provider services in the world." At the same time, he noted, damage caused by kinetic attacks could cause certain providers to "go dark" while repairs took place. Meanwhile, Ukrainian lawmaker Oleksandr Fediienko, who is a member of the parliamentary Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence, posted similar sentiments on the social network Facebook: "Will the internet disappear in Ukraine? Of course not. The infrastructure will be restructured, and alternative sites will be established." He added that the Russian attacks made no sense because Ukrainian providers were able to restore service so quickly. Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Serhii Beskrestnov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's advisor on defense technology, said that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian data centers were part of a wider campaign. "They've already been scaring us with claims that there won't be food or fuel, and now they're scaring us with the prospect of losing internet access," he wrote on Facebook. How can data and devices be protected? Glushchenko said that even if a server was destroyed, its data would be available from other data centers where it was stored, including abroad. "The system can automatically switch to a different data center," he explained. He pointed out that telecommunications companies also stored copies with cloud services offered by providers such as Google and Amazon. What happens when data centers lose power? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Oleksandr Olshanskyi, the founder of the Ukrainian web hosting provider MiroHost and also the head of the leading Ukrainian IT service company Internet Invest, told the Ukrainian news agency RBC-Ukraine that his data center had been almost totally destroyed but that this had not made a major difference. He said that the vast majority of his clients remained unaffected, as they could fall back on operation capacities in Poland and the Czech Republic. "I'm only left with about 150 out of 20,000 to 25,000 clients, who for some reason did not shift, duplicate or secure their data," he explained. Tech experts have recommended that Ukrainian data centers place a higher priority on decentralization, saying they should be as spread out as possible geographically, and also that data should be cloned and secured in other data centers abroad. Moving infrastructure into underground spaces could also be a solution, but this would translate into extra costs for customers. "We've grown accustomed to having the fastest and cheapest internet in Europe, and the best technical support," Fediienko said but pointed out that this was "about to change." Beskrestnov also expected the price of internet services to rise soon, to cover the costs of repairing damage to infrastructure. This article was originally published in Ukrainian. INTERNATIONAL Vessel containing twenty three Indians attacked, now rescued By: Agencies Date: October 8, 2026 Share post: WhatsApp Facebook X ReddIt Telegram Linkedin Moscow, Oct 7: A Liberia-flagged vessel carrying oil, with a crew of 23 Indian nationals, came under attack by drone boats off Russia’s Black Sea coast, Russian authorities said. “The crew has been saved and evacuated to shore,” a spokesman for the Russian transport ministry told state-run TASS news agency. The Aframax Rio tanker came under attack on Tuesday by unmanned surface vessels (USVs), and open fire is raging in the Black Sea waters, the Russian transport ministry said. The ministry said the vessel’s all Indian crew of 23 was saved and none was hurt according to preliminary data. The incident took place near Sochi, Russia’s popular resort city on the Black Sea coast. Russia’s Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin held a headquarters meeting on eliminating the consequences of the attack on the tanker Aframax Rio off the Black Sea coast. According to the report, the fire was so intense that firefighting could not begin initially. Open burning of oil is currently taking place in the Black Sea area. Firefighting can begin only after the intensity decreases, when it becomes possible for rescue vessels to approach the tanker safely, the report said. As a precautionary measure, Sochi Mayor Andrey Proshunin temporarily banned access to the city’s beaches. “The city’s emergency response centre has made a decision to temporarily ban access to the beaches and sea embankments. Sochi residents and guests are kindly requested not to expose to risks and wait for an official decision regarding their reopening,” Proshunin wrote on his Telegram channel. 3 Indians rescued after strike on Black Sea ship Three Indian nationals rescued from a Turkish-owned cargo vessel after a Russian drone strike in the Black Sea are in “stable condition” and have been assured of all necessary assistance for their “safe and early departure from Romania”, the Indian mission said. An embassy representative on Tuesday visited the three Indians rescued from the MV Royad Mammadov. Two of them are staying at a hotel, while the third is undergoing treatment. https://marxist.com/in-memory-of-jim-bro.text: Details Alan Woods 12 October 2026 Share Tweet The news of the death of comrade Jim Brookshaw came as a cruel blow to all of us who knew and loved him. Jim passed away on 6 October in a hospital bed, with his son Ben at his side. For the last period of his life, he had been suffering from a serious illness that undermined his health and finally claimed his life. For me personally, the news of his death was particularly painful, as Jim and I had been close friends and comrades for many years – half a century, in fact. Paradoxically, the first years of our relationship could hardly be described as friendly. In fact, we found ourselves locked in quite a sharp political conflict, as I will explain. First however, a few words should be said about Jim’s early life. The early years Jim was from Sussex, a predominantly agricultural area, which had always voted Conservative in every general election up to 1964, when the first Labour MP was elected for Kemptown Labour Party in Brighton. There were several areas like Crawley and East Grinstead where there was a strong working class. But the little village where Jim was born was not one of them. Warnham is a small and picturesque village in the Horsham district of West Sussex. Hardly a hotbed of the class struggle. Nevertheless, even in the most remote and conservative areas, the spirit of the class struggle remains alive, and workers and young people can develop very radical ideas, precisely rebelling against the prevailing mood of rural backwardness and conservatism. After the Second World War, his father, Fred Brookshaw, worked at Warnham Brickworks – a very hard and unpleasant place to work in. His mother Maud was from Durham, from a mining family. This was the class background into which Jim was born in 1941, the eldest of seven children. He had a sister, Margaret, who sadly passed away this year. Then there were Mary, David, Patricia, Jeffrey and Sally. With such a large family and low wages, it must have been a constant struggle to survive. Yet the few times that Jim ever spoke about his childhood years, it was always of happy memories of a very warm and caring family. These memories stayed with him all his life. They were the seedbed upon which arose a very powerful sense of class identity, something that he and I always had in common and which acted as a powerful bond between us. It was this powerful spirit of class consciousness that drew Jim inevitably into the camp of socialism and communism from a very young age. After leaving school, he wanted to join the navy, but his dad wouldn’t let him, insisting that he must get a trade. So he trained as a plumber, which he never liked, even though he was very good at all kinds of manual work. Leaving home, he found jobs in industry and became involved in active trade unionism. Searching for a radical expression for his instinctive class consciousness, he first joined the Young Socialists (YS) – the youth organisation of the Labour Party. From the 2009 World School of the International Marxist Tendency. Jim can be seen in the centre of the back row with his partner Hazel, to the left of him. At that time, the YS was a battleground for rival sectarian groups, like the International Socialists (now the SWP) and the Socialist Labour League, or SLL as it was commonly known, the ultra-left Healyite organisation. Alienated by the barren atmosphere of sectarianism, this young worker left the YS in disgust, eventually joining the Communist Party (CPGB) and the Young Communist League (YCL), where he soon rose to a leading position. First meeting, first clashes I first met Jim when I was a student at Sussex University, and when he was a leading figure in the local YCL in Brighton. After moving from South Wales to Sussex in the autumn of 1963, I succeeded in establishing a group at the university, which soon acquired a very powerful position. It goes without saying that we were convinced supporters of the ideas of Leon Trotsky. Jim, by contrast, could fairly be described as an equally convinced Stalinist of the hardest of hard lines. The battle lines were therefore soon drawn up between two mutually antagonistic political lines. The conflict became extremely sharp when a group of youngsters (the leaders were from Southampton) set up a branch of the Communist Party at Sussex University. But they proved completely incapable of answering the arguments of revolutionary Marxists. We defeated them politically at every turn, and they became increasingly demoralised. Becoming aware of the danger, the Communist Party in Brighton instructed them not to have any dealings with us – an instruction that they followed with blind loyalty, even refusing to say ‘good morning’ to us. But there was a problem. They participated in the University Socialist Society, which our tendency completely controlled. This meant that they had to defend the ideas of the Communist Party (which had now become completely reformist, as shown by their policy document, The British Road to Socialism ). A decisive turning point was when they got the general secretary of the CPGB, John Gollan, invited to speak at the Sussex University Socialist Society. The university Communist members sat silently, watching with horror as the party’s leading comrade was systematically demolished by the power of our arguments. In the end, Gollan, unable to answer politically, completely lost his temper and left in a fit of rage and frustration. This sad spectacle finally demolished any illusions the comrades had in the leadership of the CPGB. They said nothing to us, but we learned subsequently that at the summer camp of the YCL, they were putting up posters of Trotsky in their tent. Finally, one day, to our great surprise, they finally surrendered and came over to us en bloc . Witch hunt The local Communist Party officials immediately reacted by closing the university branch of the party and instructing all its members to join the Young Communist League in Brighton. This suited us just fine. The comrades conducted very efficient work in the YCL and won over the entire branch with the exception of the chairman and one or two others. The branch secretary was none other than Jim Brookshaw, who reacted in typical Stalinist manner, expelling practically the entire branch. Since Jim was at that time the National Chairman of the YCL, this was a most humiliating defeat. And he held me personally responsible for it! I had previously tried to win him over. I went to his house and argued furiously over a plate of beans on toast. But neither he could convince me, nor I him. The battle lines were therefore drawn. But despite the sharpness of the struggle, I never developed a sense of animosity towards Jim, a fact that he later recognised with gratitude. Later on, I discovered with surprise that Jim regarded what had happened as a kind of ‘coup’. I do not know what the basis of this accusation was, but according to him our comrades behaved very badly. I do not know how far this was true, or merely the reflection of Jim’s understandable feelings of resentment at having lost control of his branch. Some of our comrades were at times a bit frivolous and immature in their conduct, a tendency which we always tried to rectify. But the fact remains that they did have a majority in the branch, while Jim only had the support of his wife, Marion, and I think one other. Jim himself admitted that his conduct was sometimes a bit ‘thuggish’. The comrades would come to me quite often, complaining bitterly about his aggressive behaviour. But I would answer, “Jim is a worker and he is loyal to his party. We must accept that fact, and try to convince him politically.” To tell the truth, I never believed that was possible. But I was wrong. How we came together When I left Sussex, I lost all contact with Jim Brookshaw for a couple of years. But I learned that he was now working full-time for the YCL. Then one day, I was surprised to see Jim on the BBC television news. At the time, there was a major conflict between Britain and Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe). The white racists who were in power had issued a unilateral declaration of independence and hoisted their flag over the embassy building in London. On the TV screens, you could see dim pictures of a young man climbing up the side of Rhodesia House in Trafalgar Square and throwing the flag down from the top. It was a very high building and it was a very risky thing to do. Later on, Jim, with his characteristic honesty, laughingly said that, halfway up, he had second thoughts: “I was absolutely shitting myself. I went to the top of the civil service stores. You could walk from the top of that building to Rhodesia House." The flagpole was in the corner and there were ropes around it. But, having got so far, he thought it better to finish the job. “So I slithered down this roof until I got to this wide gutter. So I just go up to the flagpole, pulled it down, cut it down, and threw it, as suggested by the Morning Star , into the street. It landed at the foot of some copper apparently.” This act showed him to be a very courageous and determined individual. I took mental note of it, and thought no more about it. A mysterious letter A couple of years later, when I was working full-time for the Militant in South Wales, I was visiting our centre in London when a comrade said to me: “Alan, there is a letter for you.” This news surprised me. A letter for me, sent to the London centre? Who could it be from? I opened the letter and was frankly astonished to see that the sender was none other than Jim Brookshaw! In his letter, Jim unexpectedly announced that he had broken with Stalinism and wished to discuss with me. I lost no time, and went straight to his flat in South London (I think it was in Charlton). I remained there for two whole days, during which I had intensive discussions with Jim and his wife on just about every aspect of the international labour movement from the First International onwards. How Jim broke with Stalinism In the years since I lost contact with him, a lot of water had flowed under the bridge. The world had been shaken by great events, particularly the Hungarian Revolution of 1956, which shook every Communist Party in the world to its foundations. Many thousands of experienced communist cadres left the Party in disgust at the events in Budapest. But Jim was not among them. I am sure he had some serious doubts about it. But he remained firm in his loyalty to the Party. When I say that I am sure he had doubts, I am basing myself on things he himself told me over the years about his personal experience. Jim had now risen to quite a prominent position in the YCL, and as a trusted full-timer, he was sent on many delegations to the Soviet-led states in Eastern Europe. I remember that he went on official visits to Czechoslovakia and East Germany, but I cannot remember him mentioning visiting Moscow. Two incidents that he told me about stick in my mind. On one occasion, he was invited, along with other international delegates, to an official banquet, at which every table was decorated by the national flag of the country the delegates came from. Upon approaching the table of the British delegation, Jim was surprised and disgusted to see the Union Jack placed in a prominent position on the table. He immediately called over the official representative to complain. The explanation came back that every delegation was assigned its own national flag. And that the Party Committee had decided that this decision must be carried out. Outraged by this bureaucratic highhandedness, Jim raised such a scandal that the Party officials had never witnessed before: “I don’t care who has made the decision. You tell the Committee that I refuse to sit by a table in the presence of that disgusting reactionary rag.” Eventually the offending object had to be removed, but this little lesson was a clear indication to him that the internationalism of the so-called Communist Parties was more apparent than real. This lesson was underlined in practice a few years later, when Soviet tanks rolled into Prague in 1968 in order to crush the attempt of CP leader Alexander Dubček to reform the government and state. This made an even greater impact on Jim than the earlier events in Hungary in 1956, and it got him thinking seriously about the real nature of Stalinism, which up to then, he had staunchly defended. What’s on the menu, comrade? At these official banquets, Jim was increasingly offended by the outrageous greed of so-called ‘communist’ cadres, whose main concern appeared to be to feast and booze at the expense of the workers’ state they happen to be visiting. He cited one incident, which I believe occurred in East Germany, where he was having lunch at a factory. International delegates were served a very nice course of the best quality steak. However, Jim (who was highly observant, and far from stupid) noticed something strange. All the workers were coming into the canteen with plates of soup on their trays. Not a trace of steak in sight! He called over the Party factory official and asked him to explain this apparent discrepancy. The latter immediately pointed out that there were actually not one, but two menus – one (with steak) more expensive, and the other (with soup) cheaper. And the workers obviously preferred the latter to the former. Jim might have been satisfied with this explanation. But to his surprise, five minutes later, all the workers came in carrying the best-quality steak on their trays. Problem solved! Growing doubts These and other experiences gradually increased Jim’s doubts. However, he did not communicate these doubts to his colleagues, fearing their reaction. Instead, he began visiting the Marx Memorial Library in Clerkenwell Green, London, where he began to read anything by Trotsky that was available there. Whether the librarians (who I imagine would be veteran CP members) were suspicious of this sudden interest in Trotsky by a Party full-timer, I cannot say. But he began to read other works, particularly Lenin and Trotsky: What They Really Stood For , which made a big impression on him, and later Trotsky’s Revolution Betrayed . By reading this ‘subversive’ material, Jim’s suspicion was confirmed: a radical gulf separated Stalinism from genuine Bolshevik-Leninism. His transition from Stalinism to Trotskyism had now reached the point of no return. I listened with more interest than ever to everything Jim had to say. I was impressed by his obvious honesty. Nevertheless, the transformation of a former Stalinist bureaucrat – the man who had conducted a ferocious witch hunt against our comrades in the Brighton YCL – to Trotskyism seemed so unlikely, that I needed my opinion to be confirmed. In those days, there were no mobile phones, so in order to ring the centre, I had to leave Jim’s house and make a call from a public phone box. I asked Ted Grant to come straight away to Jim’s flat and listened to what he had to say. Ted immediately agreed, and he was convinced – as I was – of the absolute sincerity of both Jim and his wife, Marion, who apparently took the initiative to encourage him to contact me. The rest, as they say, is history. Why did he join us? One thing, however, needs to be clarified. Why did he join us? After all, there were many organisations claiming to stand for Trotskyism, and ours was by no means the largest. So why did he choose us? He gave us the answer himself. He said the following: “When I was breaking with Stalinism, I considered all the available options. I thought of the International Socialist group (now the SWP), but rejected them because of their obviously petty-bourgeois character. “The Healyites were entirely ruled out because of their extreme sectarianism and hooligan tactics, which I had witnessed firsthand in the YS. “Then I thought of you comrades, and I realised that I had treated you very badly, but that you always treated me as

Beállítom „Nagyon boldog vagyok, hogy vendégül láthatom Orbán Viktort, a barátomat, a testvéremet. Jól fogjuk érezni magunkat itt, az apám házában” – mondja X-en közzétett videójában Aleksandar Vučić. A bukott szerb vezető szerint ugyan mind a ketten nemrég veszítették el a választást, de „nem veszítették el a méltóságukat, a büszkeségüket és a hitüket”. Orbán szerint a barátok mindig barátok maradnak. „Az igaz barátok még jobb barátok is lesznek a nehéz időkben, és Aleksandar, te magad biztos lehetsz benne, hogy én mindig melletted leszek” – mondja a volt miniszterelnök. „Plusz tudod, hogy ez több volt, mint barátság kettőnk között: nagy teljesítmény volt, hogy fejlesztettük a kapcsolatokat, a testvériességet Magyarország és Szerbia között.” „Vissza fogunk jönni” – zárta a videót Vučić. Orbán Viktor Vučić mellett a Vajdasági Magyarok Szövetségének elnökével, Pásztor Bálinttal is találkozott Belgrádban. „A barátok barátok maradnak” – írta Pásztor közös fotójuk mellé a Facebookon. Szerbiában a vasárnapi előrehozott parlamenti választáson Vučić és a Szerb Haladó Párt ellenfele, az Egyetemista Lista szerezte meg a legtöbb szavazatot, a voksok mintegy 53 százalékát. Vučić vezette Egyesült Szerbia választási lista a második helyen végzett 39 százalékkal, így 14 év után először nem a Szerb Haladó Párt fogja kormányozni az országot. A volt köztársasági elnök még a választás éjszakáján elismerte vereségét , ami örömünnepet eredményezett Belgrádban. A helyszínen készült videónkat itt tudja megnézni. Vučić a veresége után arról beszélt egy interjúban, hogy Orbánnal együtt küzd a visszatérésért , és szerinte két éven belül sikerrel jár. Miután Orbán Viktor visszatért október végi párizsi útjáról , pénteken Milorad Dodiknál, a boszniai Szerb Köztársaság volt elnökénél járt, akivel egymást átkarolva pálinkáztak a tűz mellett. Milorad Dodik tavaly távozott a boszniai Szerb Köztársaság elnöki posztjáról, noha előtte sokáig nem volt hajlandó elismerni, hogy a Bosznia-Hercegovina bírósága jogerős ítéletben fosztotta meg őt mandátumától.
